newsitem.title: USA: House rejects eased species law for flood control.
newsitem.headline: House rejects eased species law for flood control.

text.p: The House of Representatives on Wednesday rejected a measure to exempt most flood control activities, such as maintaining levees and operating dams, from federal requirements to protect endangered wildlife.
Instead the House voted 227-196 in favour of a compromise bill to allow swift flood control repairs in emergencies without interference from the Endangered Species Act.

The White House threatened to veto the more sweeping bill, saying it was unnecessary and so broad it would exempt operations of an array of projects such as Hoover and Grand Coulee dams and the Columbia River Basin from laws to protect endangered salmon and other wildlife.

"This bill would gut the Endangered Species Act, make no mistake about that," said New York Republican Sherwood Boehlert, who sponsored the compromise measure that puts into law emergency policies federal agencies already follow.
"Protections for salmon, whooping cranes, manatees and other creatures would not be possible," Boehlert said.

But Alaska Republican Don Young, a co-sponsor of the broader bill, complained that Boehlert's substitute would only allow quick flood control repairs "if an emergency has struck or is threatening," and called it an amendment "that does nothing, absolutely zero."

Republican Richard Pombo, another sponsor of the broader bill, said flood damage in his central California district was worsened last year by levees that could not be maintained properly because of federal protections for an endangered beetle that lived in bushes on the levees.
The Army Corps of Engineers disputed Pombo's argument, and said the levees simply gave way to an uncontrollable volume of water.
Pombo has long advocated revamping endangered wildlife protections to give more weight to private property rights and economic development.
"This is nothing more than to blow a hole in the Endangered Species Act that far exceeds holes blown in the levees," California Democrat George Miller said.
But Idaho Republican Helen Chenoweth said: "When are we going to put humans and human property above the lives of a beetle or a snail?"
Pombo had hoped to tuck his measure into an emergency bill to provide disaster relief for 23 states, including the flood-ravaged upper Midwest, a move the White House said it opposed.
Idaho Republican Sen. Larry Craig was expected Thursday to attempt to put a narrower version of Pombo's bill in the Senate's emergency funding bill.
